extracted.intended_audience: literate public and political reformers in late-18th-century Britain (readers of a political pamphlet)
extracted.subtask_description: A late‑18th‑century political pamphlet arguing normative standards for governments (taxation, representation, commerce, institutions) and advocating reforms; aimed at persuading the public and motivating revolution/reform. Contains normative claims about what constitutes just government and good public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct roles of civil vs. cabinet (foreign) government
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two distinct characters of government: the civil government (government of laws) which operates at home and with little charge, and the court or cabinet government which operates abroad on an uncivilised plan and is attended with boundless extravagance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine argues that civil government alone produces little pretence for many taxes because it operates 'directly under the eye of the country' while uncivilised foreign/opera­tions enlarge pretences for power and revenue. If the foreign/cabinet part were removed the civil government would continue; revolutions aim to change this moral condition so public taxes lessen. Examples: administration by magistrates, juries, assize vs. expensive foreign intrigues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce as a pacific force and means to civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce is a pacific system that cordialises mankind by rendering nations useful to each other; permitted to act universally it would extirpate the system of war and produce a revolution toward civilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commerce is described as reciprocal—only half its power resides within one nation—and interruptions (war, piracy, broken channels) reduce commerce everywhere. Promoting civil intercourse by exchange of benefits is philosophically and politically valuable. Practical implication: encourage free commerce rather than foreign dominion or war. Anti-patterns: protectionist/naval militarisation and colonial dominion that disrupt trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of trade accounting is fallacious
rubrics_metrics.description: The custom-house 'balance of trade' figures mislead because exports appear as profits while losses at sea and foreign failures are counted as exports, and smuggling imports are omitted; thus custom-house books cannot prove a national advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine uses concrete accounting criticisms (Mr. Pitt's customs balance, omitted smuggling, losses counted on wrong side) to show that the notion of a national balance of trade as a superior advantage is false and misleading. Policy implication: do not base national policy on such misinterpreted records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign dominion and naval expense are unprofitable and destructive of national wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce connected with foreign dominion is the most unprofitable; the expense of maintaining dominion and navies more than absorbs profits of trade and lessens the mass of wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine argues that dominion cannot engross commerce and necessarily breaks out; the costs of dominion and navies, when subtracted from trade profits, show dominion to be injurious. He calls navies for commerce 'delusive'—they are 'means of destruction' not protection. Policy implication: relinquish costly foreign dominion and naval pretences in favor of free commercial intercourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charters and corporations are instruments of exclusion that take away rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A charter does not give rights but takes rights away by excluding the majority; rights are inherent, and charters operate by annulling rights of many and leaving rights to a few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine describes charters as indirectly negative: they make a difference in favour of A by taking away the right of B. He criticises charters' effects on voting, local naturalisation by purchase, and feudal-like exclusion. Examples and consequences: restricted freedom of residence, hindered population movement, and the need to abolish or reform such instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporations depress towns, property, and commerce by preventing settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations and municipal charters prevent free settlement, discourage population growth, and thereby lessen property value and national commerce; corporation towns are often in solitary decay except where geography offsets the harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine cites Manchester, Birmingham, Sheffield contrasted with corporation towns; population is a chief source of wealth and anything preventing it reduces land value. Policy implication: encourage freedom of settlement and remove municipal restrictions/fees that block newcomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate-controlled elections corrupt representation and produce unfit legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: Many parliamentary seats come from corporations; the mode of entering Parliament by corporate boroughs disciplines candidates to corruption, meaning representatives are unlikely to be men of moral honour and just legislative qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine argues that corrupt electoral origins produce corrupt legislatures. He notes the need for candidates to submit to 'mean drudgery and disgraceful arts' to be elected in corporation-influenced boroughs. Reform implication: abolish or reform corporation-based franchises and rotten/closed boroughs to secure better representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: A legislative house composed of a single class (House of Peers) is unjust and self‑protecting
rubrics_metrics.description: A house of legislation composed entirely of men of one class (landed aristocracy) functions as a combination in a common interest, designed to protect that interest (e.g., ward off taxes) rather than the common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine contends there is no special reason for a separate legislative chamber to be made up of landholders; its practical use is to avoid taxes and throw burdens onto others. He analyses tax history and policy effects, arguing that such class-based chambers create systemic inequality. Reform implication: legislative composition should not privilege a single economic class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation has become excessive due to foreign wars, dominion, and corruption; taxes should be lessened
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes rose enormously (Paine provides historical annual tax figures) and have not been reduced because of extravagance, corruption, and secret continental intrigues; the people must be watchful to lessen the burden of taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine gives seven-century tax figures and attributes the sharp rise to the Hanover succession, continental intrigues, and war. He argues that taxes once were taken off and can be reduced again by reform. Policy implication: increase transparency and curb secret expenditures; reduce foreign adventurism that increases taxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation must be equitable — consumption taxes disproportionately burden the poor and exempt the aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes on consumption (e.g., beer duties) fall heaviest on the poor and are often structured so the aristocracy are exempt (they brew their own beer); consumption taxes plus poor-rates punish the lower classes while the land-tax has been favoured less on the privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine provides examples and figures (beer tax nearly equals land-tax) and reasons: poorer classes consume more taxable articles proportionately and live in towns where poor-rates rise. Reform implication: design tax systems that do not shift burdens unfairly onto the poor and that do not allow privileged exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primogeniture and hereditary privileges are unjust
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of primogeniture is denounced as 'a law of brutal injustice' and an attaint upon character; inheritable privileges that preserve aristocratic wealth are morally indefensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine rejects the claimed social 'weight and consequence' of primogeniture, calling it privateering on family property and arguing it does not produce true national consequence. Reform implication: change inheritance laws that perpetuate aristocratic privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crown as an expensive nominal office and obsolete executive form
rubrics_metrics.description: The crown signifies a nominal office consuming large public revenue with business consisting merely in receiving money; whether the person is wise or not matters little, and the office chiefly serves to hood‑wink the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine argues the term 'executive' is outdated because the judicial/executive roles have shifted; the crown's maintenance increases expenses and relies on superstition. Reform implication: curtail costly ceremonial offices and make executive power accountable and meaningful rather than nominal and expensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil government should provide education for youth and support for the aged to prevent crime and profligacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil government does not consist in executions but in making provision for instruction of youth and support of age to exclude profligacy and despair; failure to do so produces crime and creates those executed or in workhouses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine links social misery and public punishment: youth bred without morals and the aged unsupported become victims of 'vice and legal barbarity.' He argues resources wasted on courts and luxury could instead reform these evils. Policy implication: allocate public funds to education and social supports rather than to extravagant court spending.
